newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU grain cut plans seen raising howls of protest.
newsitem.headline: EU grain cut plans seen raising howls of protest.

text.p: Grain producers and most EU farm ministers are expected to strongly oppose plans to compensate farmers for only half of a planned 20 percent cut in cereals intervention prices, agriculture analysts said on Wednesday.
Under draft plans obtained by Reuters on Tuesday, the EU cereals intervention price would be cut in one step to 95.35 Ecus a tonne in 2000 from 119.19 Ecus in 1997/98.
But compensation -- a non-crop specific area payment paid directly to farmers -- would only be raised to 66 Ecus a tonne from 54.34 Ecus.
The cut in the guaranteed price of about 24 Ecus a tonne would be partially offset by increased aid of 12 Ecus a tonne.
"It breaks the promise made under the 1992 EU farm reforms to fully compensate farmers for price cuts," said one analyst, adding that farm ministers would almost certainly ease the cuts.

Reductions in grain prices and farmers' compensation are part of a series of farm reform proposals European Commission President Jacques Santer is expected to unveil to the European Parliament in Strasbourg next Wednesday.
The farm reforms are part of a three-part package that would also examine the impact of enlargement eastwards on EU regional and social spending and set budget guidelines from 1999 to 2005.
On Wednesday, the European Commission's chief spokesman, Nikolaus van der Pas, declined to comment on the draft plans, saying the figures were likely to be changed.
For instance, the compensation figure was put at 78 Ecus a tonne under a recent draft but has now been trimmed by 12 Ecus a tonne following pressure from agriculture and budgetary aides.
EU Farm Commissioner Franz Fischler has argued that cereals producers have been heavily over-paid -- by an estimated 8.5 billion Ecus over the past four years.
The payments were intended to compensate farmers for a 30 percent cut in cereals intervention prices agreed under 1992 farm reforms aimed at removing costly farm surpluses.
But market prices soared above EU intervention levels after drought and floods hit crops across the world and stocks plunged to a 20-year low.
Commission sources sought to play down moves to cut aid to cereals farmers, saying they were unlikely to bite.
"You can't assume that market prices will fall (below intervention)," one said.
The aim was to cut intervention prices to around world prices so as to make EU farmers competitive and to export as much as possible without subsidies, the source added.
The Commission's draft said EU internal grain prices could be expected to remain above world prices up to 2005.
European agriculture industry sources noted some estimates which saw EU grain prices remaining 12 to 13 percent above EU intervention levels.
"In this case such a big intervention price cut is not needed," one said.
The sources rejected Fischler's claim of over-compensation, saying most cereals farmers did not benefit.

They said the claim was based on payments to British farmers due to the pound's depreciation in recent years, drought aid to Spanish and Portuguese farmers and aid for feed grains, mainly maize, to compensate dairy farmers for price cuts planned under 1992 reforms that never happened.
